title: Slow AI & How to Improve Student Thinking
author: Matt Hutson
summary: Matt Hutson, a teacher and writer, reflects on Sam Illingworth's book Slow AI through the question of what happens to learning when AI makes an assignment easier to finish. He argues that friction is where thought happens and cites the Bastani study in which students using a general chatbot scored about 17 percent lower once the tool was removed, while a safeguarded tutor largely erased the penalty. He also notes encouraging results for a designed physics tutor and warns that sycophantic AI feedback and unverified time savings can mislead. On assessment he distrusts AI detectors, citing false positives against non-native English writers, and prefers conversations about process, notes and revision. He ends with his CARE method of Clarify, Articulate, Refine, Execute, which keeps human thinking first, and with a prompt to pause before each AI request and ask whether it makes room for thinking or rushes past it.
points: Some difficulty is the learning itself, so teachers should ask what a friction point is doing before an AI tool removes it.

In the cited high school maths study, unrestricted chatbot practice raised assisted scores but left students about 17 percent worse once the tool was withdrawn, while a hint-based tutor avoided the loss.
Chatbot praise is often unreliable, so Hutson asks AI for the strongest argument against his view and then verifies the objection himself.
Detector verdicts should not trigger automatic zeros; conversations about drafts, evidence choices and revisions give better evidence of what a student learned.
His CARE method (Clarify, Articulate, Refine, Execute) puts the learner's own thinking before AI help and ends with using the understanding.
quotes: The question I kept returning to was this: When AI makes an assignment easier to finish, what happens to the learning the assignment was supposed to produce?
What worries me most is that students might hand over skills they haven't developed yet. You cannot lose something you never gained in the first place.
Both AI groups did better during assisted practice. However, once the tools were removed, students with the general chatbot scored about 17% lower than those who practiced without AI.
Before removing a difficulty, I want to know what it is doing. Is it preventing someone from participating, or is working through it part of what they need to learn?
With AI, a useful request is: “Give me the strongest argument against what I just said.” Or, “What would a critical reviewer notice?
I want to measure the whole process, including the repairs, rather than celebrate how quickly the first version appeared.
If I encounter writing that raises questions, I do not want my first response to be an automatic zero. I want a conversation.
